newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: INTERVIEW - Goudsmit says acquistions key to growth.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Goudsmit says acquistions key to growth.

text.p: Dutch employment and educational services group Goudsmit is looking to more than double its turnover to 300 million guilders by the year 2000 as it targets acquisitions both at home and abroad, chairman Rob van den Hoek said on Monday.

"In the long term, I think it will become necessary to look outside our borders in order to ensure our continuity," he told Reuters in an interview, adding the company would start screening foreign takeover candidates in 1998.
"But we have to ensure we don't grow too fast, we must keep our expansion under control."
And despite tough competition and pressure on margins, Van den Hoek saw further growth beyond the turn of the century.
"I think there'll still be quite a way to go once we've reached the 300 (million guilders turnover)," he said.

Goudsmit's turnover in 1996 was 122.9 million guilders from 83.63 million in 1993, while operating profit climbed to 13.19 million guilders from 2.05 million during the same period. Van den Hoek expects turnover to rise to between 180 million to 200 million guilders this year, aided by recent acquisitions.
Over the last couple of years Goudsmit has refocused its activities, selling its retail chains -- the last one in 1996 -- and now concentrates on employment and educational services.
Net profit soared to 11.11 million guilders in 1996, 65 percent above 1995's.
Despite stagnation in the home market for technical temporary employment, Goudsmit was diversified enough to ensure a good profit outlook, Van den Hoek said.
"Only some 10 percent of turnover is generated by pure technical temping, the rest is technical employment on a project basis and by education," he said.
Goudsmit runs a network of 13 private schools, mostly in the Netherlands, but one in Belgium.
He said Goudsmit's technical project units -- well-known within the industrial engineering sector -- were a substantial advantage.
"Some of our units, such as Edes Seagull and Polec, have existed some 30 years. People turn to them when they're looking for a highly trained technical personnel," he said.
Edes Seagull, Polec and this year's Belgian acquisition Edora all offer technical employees on a project basis.
Edora and Edes Seagull are active in the petrochemical and chemical industries, and Polec offers achitectural and engineering staff. Other units cover civil engineering and telecommunications.
Goudsmit foresees growth for all units in 1997.
